The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The fighters’ four-fifths were then divided among them according to a system of ranks that combined tribal status with something like class status.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Second, non-Muslims—Christians, Jews, and Ṣābiʾans, the groups known as the People of the Book—were required to pay the jizya tax.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Those who paid this tax were known as ahl al-dhimma, the protected people.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The term meant that once the war of conquest had ended, or once an agreement had been made with the local population and they had accepted payment of the jizya, Christians and Jews in these countries came under Arab protection.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

This protection covered their lives, their private property, their personal and religious freedoms, and their right to continue practicing the rituals and customs they had followed before the Arab conquest.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This gives us another reason to reject the theory mentioned earlier that religious fanaticism was the main cause of the Arab conquests.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It also shows that spreading Islam was not an independent goal cut off from the social aims we have just discussed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

We will later see that some Arab rulers in the conquered countries actually discouraged local people from becoming Muslims when they realized that conversion reduced the amount of jizya entering the public treasury.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Muslims, and people who converted to Islam from other religions, did not have to pay this tax.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Third, the jizya brought enormous sums of money to the Arab conquerors.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was said that under ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Egypt alone sent around fourteen million gold dinars to the caliphal treasury, while Iraq sent one hundred million silver dirhams.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

In the early period of conquest, Byzantine gold currency remained in use in the lands that had previously been under Byzantine rule, while Persian silver currency continued to be used in Iraq and the Persian provinces.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Fourth, when one of the protected non-Muslims converted to Islam, the jizya was removed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Instead, the convert became subject to the Muslim obligation of zakāt, which was lower in both amount and rate than the jizya.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
If a non-Muslim peasant converted to Islam and then left the countryside for the city, he had to pay zakāt.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
If he remained in the countryside and continued farming, he instead paid the kharāj, a land tax taken from agricultural production at a rate of one-tenth.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Most of the population in the conquered countries were peasants, because agriculture was the main form of production.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
For that reason, revenue from the kharāj formed a large part of the income of the Bayt al-Māl.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Fifth, the conversion of these populations from Christianity and other religions to Islam proceeded slowly during the early period of the conquests. The Muslim Arab conquerors did not make a deliberate effort to spread Islam through direct missionary activity.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

One reason was financial. The jizya, the tax paid by non-Muslims, brought large sums into the state treasury. This helped weaken any incentive to encourage widespread conversion in the conquered lands.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The historical sources even mention measures intended to limit the number of local people converting to Islam. As increasing numbers of the protected non-Muslim population entered Islam, revenue from the jizya began to fall.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Al-Balādhurī, for example, reports that officials serving al-Ḥajjāj, the Umayyad governor of Iraq, wrote to complain about this very problem:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“The land-tax revenue has fallen, and the protected non-Muslims have converted to Islam and moved to the cities.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They meant that these people had converted, left agricultural work in the countryside, and moved into the towns. As a result, the state lost revenue from both the land tax, or kharāj, and the jizya.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

What matters here is that large numbers of people entering Islam became a cause for complaint. That complaint tells us something important: the state’s financial income came first, while the conversion of the population came second.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Sixth, the term “protected peoples” originally referred specifically to Christians and Jews, whom the Qurʾān calls the “People of the Book”—that is, the followers of the Torah and the Gospel, or more generally the followers of earlier revealed religions recognized by Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Later, however, the Arab conquerors broadened this category in their treatment of local populations. Some caliphs extended it to include the Sabians and Zoroastrians as well. This was done through legal interpretation, and the purpose was to increase the number of people liable to pay the jizya and therefore increase the revenue it produced.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

We can therefore say that the Arab conquerors’ lack of interest in rapidly expanding the Muslim population of the conquered lands had a material basis. The same material basis can also help explain the religious tolerance that marked Arab rule in this period.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Seventh, from the beginning of the conquests, the Arabs established special military settlements for their armies. These were known as amṣār, with each individual settlement called a miṣr.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

These settlements later became major centers of intellectual, economic, and political life in the Arab state. Among them were Basra and Kufa in Iraq, both founded during the rule of the second caliph, ʿUmar; Fusṭāṭ in Egypt, today Cairo, also founded during ʿUmar’s rule; and Kairouan in Tunisia, founded during the rule of Muʿāwiya, the founder of the Umayyad state.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The first striking feature of these towns is that they were laid out along tribal lines. Each was divided into quarters, and each tribe was assigned its own quarter, which then took the tribe’s name.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The second striking feature is that many of the wealthy merchants of Mecca—men who had already been rich before Islam and had become highly skilled in trade and profit-making—moved to Kufa and Basra. They brought their commercial activity and capital with them.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Many craftsmen followed them to work for these wealthy groups. As a result, a clear class structure began to emerge in the new towns. Agricultural labor, meanwhile, was increasingly carried out by enslaved captives and poor free workers.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The third feature was the separation of the military commanders, wealthy merchants, and other leading figures from the local population. They lived apart in these towns, which became something like isolated strongholds: military strongholds and class strongholds at the same time.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Eighth, the Arab conquerors did not follow the usual practice of conquerors in that period by looting the cities they captured.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They generally limited themselves to taking the property of wealthy people and leading notables who fled when the conquerors entered. This property included money, movable goods, slaves, and palaces.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Land itself was not taken in this way until the reign of ʿUthmān, the third caliph. Under him, Umayyad governors from among his relatives began building up large and wealthy estates at the expense of the state treasury, poor Arabs, and the poor of the conquered lands.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
What can we conclude when we bring these eight observations together?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In our view, they point to something extremely important.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

They show that religion was not the decisive force behind the Arab conquests. If we look again at each of these observations, and then consider them together, we can see that social forces played a major and often decisive role in driving the Arabs out of the Arabian Peninsula and into a much larger world filled with economic activity, social life, and diversity.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

This does not mean denying the historical role of Islam as one of the forces behind the conquests. That role was especially important for those who took part sincerely because of their commitment to Islam and their religious faith.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

But our concern here is not the personal intention of individual believers. We are looking instead for the objective force that drew people from many different tribes of the Arabian Peninsula into campaigns that were close to an adventure—if not outright adventure.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

When we analyze the historical facts we have discussed, it is difficult to believe that religion alone could have driven such large numbers of people so powerfully into battle and danger against the two strongest states in the civilized world at the time.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Alongside this first conclusion, we can draw several others from the same eight observations:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The Byzantine and Persian authorities had practiced various forms of social, religious, and sectarian persecution. When the Arab conquerors entered these lands, they presented the local population with principles and slogans that many people saw as offering hope for better living conditions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arab conquerors raised the principle that there should be no war against those willing to make peace. They also raised the principle that there should be no compulsion in religion.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

When they entered a country, its inhabitants were to receive security and protection for their lives, property, personal freedom, and religious freedom. War booty was taken only from lands whose rulers rejected peace and chose war.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The booty was limited to what was found with the rear units of enemy armies, and to the wealth and palaces of rich people and nobles who fled the cities.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Even in lands taken by force rather than through a peace agreement, the Arabs did not loot the cities or seize the property of ordinary inhabitants. The exception was the property of the wealthy and noble groups just mentioned.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The Arab conquerors allowed local Christian clergy to hold the highest religious offices in their own communities, replacing Greek clergy whom the Byzantine Church had imposed on religious institutions in Syria, Palestine, and Egypt.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This won the support of the local clergy. Some of them even became advocates of Arab rule in these countries.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In the land tax, or kharāj, the conquerors treated Arabs working in agriculture in the same way as non-Arabs.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This helped them win the support of this part of the population.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Local merchants made large profits from the conquerors because the Arabs often sold them captured goods at very low prices, even when the goods were extremely valuable.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arabs arriving from the peninsula often did not know the true value of these objects. Local merchants therefore had a strong interest in maintaining good relations with the conquerors.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At the time Islam appeared, Arab society was approaching the stage of a class society, but it had not yet reached the more developed class structure already found in the conquered lands.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
For this reason, the Arabs left the existing feudal institutions of power largely in place. At first, they neither seized those institutions nor took a direct part in running them.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Nor did the conquerors immediately enter the process of social production. They remained largely separate from it. For a time, this also kept them separate from the wider social life of the conquered countries.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

They continued to live in their military settlements—the new towns established after the conquests—and in doing so preserved many of their dominant tribal traditions. They were also afraid that the Arab element might be absorbed into the much larger non-Arab populations around them.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The feudal ruling groups in these countries therefore kept their positions and class privileges. As a result, these landholding elites had little reason to create trouble or organize counter-revolts against the Arab conquerors.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
During the conquests, another slogan appeared: the Arabs were the army of Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Under this principle, among the original inhabitants of the conquered lands, only Arabs were allowed to join the Arab armies operating there.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

This made it possible for Arab tribes that had been living in Iraq and Syria long before the conquests to join those armies. These included tribes that had once belonged to the Lakhmid state in Iraq and the Ghassanid state in Syria. Most had been Christian. Some later converted to Islam, while others remained Christian.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

In this way, the conquerors also secured the support of Arab tribes already living in the conquered lands. Their support may have come from ethnic or tribal solidarity, or from material interests, since joining the conquerors allowed them to preserve full equality with the victorious Arabs.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Taken as a whole, this picture gives the researcher a clearer view of many important historical facts—social, political, and intellectual.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

But we should remember that these observations apply only to a limited period in the history of Arab rule over the conquered lands. We can probably say that the picture began to change during the reign of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān. We will see this shortly.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One final point should be added.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Following Qurʾānic guidance and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s rules for the conduct of conquest, the Arab conquerors adopted a principle that deserves attention in both their overall strategy and their conduct in particular situations.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They were not to begin an armed conflict, and were to use force only in three cases:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The first was self-defense against an enemy:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. God does not love those who transgress.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The second was to protect the weak and save them from oppression or destruction:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

“Why should you not fight in the way of God and for the oppressed among men, women, and children, who say: ‘Our Lord, take us out of this town whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper’?”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The third was when the opposing side itself resorted to arms—that is, when the other side began the fighting:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Fight them until there is no persecution and religion belongs to God. But if they stop, then there is to be no aggression except against the wrongdoers.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“If they incline toward peace, then incline toward it as well, and put your trust in God.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
6 — The System of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Most of the system we have just described for the early Islamic conquests goes back to the second Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Drawing on the general principles of Islamic law, together with his own bold legal reasoning, ʿUmar developed a practical policy for three areas: the armies carrying out the conquests, the tribes to which the soldiers belonged, and the conquered lands themselves.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Some parts of this system were positive, while others were negative.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Among its positive features was something that, to a certain extent, can be described using Engels’s term “military democracy.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

In principle, the relationship between the commanders of the conquering armies and their soldiers rested on a fairly broad form of this democracy. In practice, however, it remained limited because tribal traditions were still powerful.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We saw this especially in the distribution of booty. The stated rules could be violated when tribal chiefs took the shares belonging to ordinary soldiers from their own tribes.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Another positive feature of ʿUmar’s system was his establishment of some of the foundations of a “state” in the legal and administrative sense.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUmar created the first dīwān in Islam. It was a form of government administration, rather like a ministry.
